stem: What is the most injured organ in abdominal blunt injuries?
expl: The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma (liver is close second, and the commonest in penetrating trauma).

why.A: Second in blunt trauma (most common in penetrating).

stem: A 22-year-old healthy patient is scheduled for a splenectomy due to hypersplenism. Which of the following is the best intervention to reduce the risk of future infections?

opts.t: Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type B

srcNote: (Spleen)
expl: Splenectomy removes protection against encapsulated organisms → vaccinate against S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis and H. influenzae b (ideally ≥2 weeks before elective surgery).

why.D: Used in selected high-risk patients (e.g. children), not the best single intervention.

stem: A patient presents with a spleen laceration measuring 2 cm. What is the injury grade?
expl: AAST spleen: grade I laceration <1 cm deep; grade II 1–3 cm parenchymal depth not involving trabecular vessels; grade III >3 cm or involving trabecular vessels.

stem: Patient done splenectomy he developed fever and rash post op
expl: Fever (± purpuric rash) after splenectomy must be treated as overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (encapsulated organisms, mainly pneumococcus) — immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics.

why.B: Pancreatic tail injury can cause pancreatitis/fistula but doesn't explain fever with rash.

stem: A 52 years old man presented to the ER department with acute hematemesis. Bleeding esophageal varices were found during upper GI endoscopy. Which one of the following is the most likely to be effective treatment for this Patient?
srcNote: (Acute and chronic pancreatitis) Source note (Final 439 F Q37): The related recall asks for management after stabilization and gives A. endoscopy therapy. Answer: A.
expl: For actively bleeding oesophageal varices, endoscopic therapy (sclerotherapy or, preferably, band ligation) controls ~90% of bleeds. Balloon tamponade is a temporary bridge; PPI and adrenaline are for ulcer bleeding.

stem: A patient with a blunt splenic injury, CT angio showed extravasation blush. The patient was hemodynamically stable. What is the next step?

opts.t: Monitor with serial CBC and Hb

expl: A haemodynamically stable patient with a contrast blush (active arterial bleeding) on CT → angioembolisation (non-operative management). Unstable → laparotomy.

why.D: Blush = high risk of failure with observation alone.

stem: A patient presented with esophageal variceal bleeding, in examination he has splenomegaly with normal portal vein and liver. What could be the cause?
expl: Varices with splenomegaly but a normal liver and portal vein = left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension from splenic vein thrombosis (often pancreatitis) — cured by splenectomy.

why.B: Pre-sinusoidal hepatic cause — periportal fibrosis on US.
why.D: A consequence of PHT, not a cause.

stem: A case about a female who experienced a car crash from her left side, and on PE they found that she has fractured ribs from the 7th to the 10th. And asks about what could be possibly injured in the patient ?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses) Incomplete choice set: options B, C and D are recorded as "??" in the source.
expl: Left lower rib fractures (7th–10th/9th–12th) are associated with splenic injury (right-sided → liver).

stem: Patient with variceal bleeding after the initial maintenance of airway, breathing, and circulation. Which intravenous medication has been shown to reduce the mortality incidence in this case?
srcNote: (Surgical infections) Source note (Final 437 B Q33): The related recall of hematemesis with jaundice and spider telangiectasia gives C. IV Antibiotics. Answer: C.
expl: In variceal bleeding (cirrhosis), prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality.

why.A: Octreotide controls bleeding but its mortality benefit is less established.

stem: a patient presented after a trauma with splenic rupture. He had a splenectomy. A year later he presented with hypotension, fever, and septic shock. What is the most likely organism?
srcNote: (Surgical infections) Encapsulated organism
expl: After splenectomy, overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is caused by encapsulated organisms — mostly Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: A young male patient, who is known to have liver cirrhosis and esophageal varices presented with complaint of vomiting blood. After initial fluid resuscitation, which one of the following is your treatment of choice for this patient?
srcNote: (Hepato-bilio-pancreatic neoplasms)
expl: After resuscitation, start a splanchnic vasoconstrictor — octreotide (or terlipressin) — plus antibiotics, before urgent endoscopy. Propranolol is for prophylaxis, not acute bleeding.

stem: Pt newly diagnosed with liver cirrhosis on endoscopy there were visible esophageal varices. How would you prevent the first bleed of the varices?
srcNote: (Hepato-bilio-pancreatic neoplasms)
expl: Primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding = non-selective β-blocker (propranolol/nadolol/carvedilol) ± band ligation.

stem: a 38-year-old woman presented to your clinic complaining of gingival bleeding and easy bruising. On taking careful history, she also mentions that she had a few episodes of epistaxis in the last two months. Investigations done and she was found to have platelets count < 10,000/mcl. Work up revealed no specific cause for the patient's thrombocytopenia. After six weeks of work up, her platelets count was 9,000/mcl. What is the best definitive therapy for this patient?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Source key B. ITP (mucocutaneous bleeding with isolated thrombocytopenia) — first-line is steroids/IVIG; splenectomy is indicated for steroid-refractory disease, platelets <10,000 for ≥6 weeks, or steroid toxicity. The recall's investigations likely showed refractory/severe disease.

stem: A 55-year-old man presented with large volume hematemesis, hypotension and reduced level of consciousness. The medical team started to resuscitate the patient with blood transfusion on physical examination, you found the patient to have jaundice and multiple spider telangiectasia. Which of the following is the appropriate next step of management?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Cirrhotic with variceal bleeding: antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) reduce infection and mortality; given early with resuscitation and vasoactive drugs.

why.A: Doesn't correct the coagulopathy of cirrhosis quickly.
why.D: For peptic ulcer bleeding (often given empirically but doesn't reduce mortality in varices).

stem: 29 years old female presented with epigastric pain and vomiting underwent endoscopy to rule out cholecystitis. No cholecystitis but a 5 cm splenic artery aneurysm was found. She is symptomatic and planning to get pregnant and there was no interventional radiologist in the hospital so the doctor decided to do elective splenectomy. When is the best timing to give vaccines prior to the operation to prevent infection by encapsulated bacteria ?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: For elective splenectomy, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae b) at least 2 weeks (2–3 weeks) before surgery so that the immune response develops while the spleen is still present. In emergency splenectomy, vaccinate ~14 days after.

why.B: The policy for emergency cases, not elective.
why.C: Too late for an antibody response.
why.D: Used only when the splenectomy was unplanned.

stem: Patient after RTA, admitted in hospital was unstable, exam found hemoperitoneum and found to have 3.5 cm hematoma on spleen. Was taken to OR and a laparotomy was done. What is the best management?
srcNote: (liver spleen disorders and pancreatic masses)
expl: An unstable patient with haemoperitoneum from a splenic injury taken to laparotomy → total splenectomy (fast, definitive). Splenic preservation is for stable patients/children.

stem: Regarding trauma and splenic laceration. Which of the following is contraindicated in non-operative management?
srcNote: (Trauma) explanation: in a small center either you do splenectomy or Transfer to a big center.
expl: Non-operative management of splenic injury needs ICU monitoring, IR, blood bank and a surgeon available 24 h. In a peripheral hospital without these, operate or transfer. High grade alone isn't an absolute contraindication if stable.

why.A: High grade isn't an absolute contraindication when stable.

stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis is at the clinic for (operative assessment). The surgeon asks you to calculate the Child-Pugh score. What element is needed to calculate the score?
srcNote: (Pre-Operative Assessment) In child-pugh score we use: albumin, total bilirubin, INR (or PT), ascites, hepatic encephalopathy.
expl: Child-Pugh = bilirubin (total), albumin, INR/PT, ascites, encephalopathy.

stem: A 38-year-old man who had a history of recurrent acute pancreatitis over the last 10 years presented to the ER complaining of frequent episodes of vomiting fresh blood for 12 hours. Intravenous resuscitation was initiated. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: isolated bleeding fundal varices which has been controlled by injection sclerotherapy. US: Splenomegaly, normal portal vein and thrombosed splenic vein. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: d (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Recurrent pancreatitis → splenic vein thrombosis → left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension → isolated gastric (fundal) varices with a normal portal vein → splenectomy is curative. (Source key "d".)

stem: A 45 year old male patient, known case liver cirrhosis and esophageal varices is brought to the hospital with history of vomiting bright red blood three times at home. On initial examination you noticed blood staining over his lips and teeth. He produces incomprehensible sounds, opens his eyes to painful stimuli and is able to localize pain. Vital sign are: Heart rate 120/min, BP: 85/60 mmHg, O2 saturation 93% on room air. After managing the airway, which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Control of bleeding using sangstaken-Blakemore tube

srcNote: ( Trauma) Source note (Midterm 430 A Q15): definitive is upper gi endoscopy and we do ligation but initial we have to stabilize and give crystalloids
expl: After securing the airway (GCS low), the hypotensive variceal bleeder needs immediate fluid resuscitation before endoscopy or balloon tamponade.

why.A: Bridge if bleeding can't be controlled endoscopically.

stem: Which ONE of the following is a post-hepatic cause of portal hypertension?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Post-hepatic (post-sinusoidal) obstruction: Budd–Chiari (hepatic vein thrombosis), constrictive pericarditis, right heart failure.

stem: A 32- year-old alcoholic male patient is brought to the emergency department with a history of vomiting large amount of bright red blood. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly and ascites. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Massive bright-red haematemesis in an alcoholic with splenomegaly and ascites (portal hypertension) → bleeding oesophageal varices.

stem: All except bleeding varices: “incomplete Q”
srcNote: Incomplete source recall. The source lists "Urgent" and "endoscopy" as separate choices; all five choices and the original key are preserved.
expl: Incomplete recall: everything listed is part of variceal-bleed care (ABC, urgent endoscopy; bilharziasis as a cause) except immediate laparotomy.

why.A: A cause of portal hypertension in our region.

stem: Esophageal varices can be treated by all except
srcNote: Year not stated
expl: Varices are treated by sclerotherapy, band ligation, balloon tamponade, drugs, TIPS. Neither cautery nor "electrotherapy" is a variceal treatment; the key is B.

stem: A 52 years old man presented to ER with acute hematemesis. Bleeding esophageal varices were found during upper GI endoscopy. The patient did not response to endoscopic treatment Bp 80/40 HR 160, which of the following is the most likely to be effective treatment for this patient?
srcNote: not known. Minnesota tube is used as a way to control bleeding not to treat. Unanswered source question: the source states "not known" and supplies only three options. Its original note is retained above.
expl: No key in the source. Variceal bleeding failing endoscopic therapy in a shocked patient → balloon tamponade (Minnesota/Sengstaken) as a temporary bridge to TIPS. (Octreotide should already be running; oesophagectomy is never done for varices.)

why.B: Should already be running; not enough alone.
